oi.text: In the third quarter of 2026, the favourable impact of fuel prices on "Operating income" was $28 million compared to the same period of 2025. Higher fuel prices, partially offset by the unfavourable impact from the timing of recoveries under the Company's fuel cost adjustment program, resulted in an increase in "Total revenues" of $244 million. Higher fuel prices net of purchasing discounts, resulted in an increase in "Total operating expenses" of $216 million.

da_op.heading: Depreciation and Amortization
da_op.text:
Depreciation and amortization expense is the charge associated with the use of track and roadway, rolling stock, buildings, and other depreciable assets, including assets related to the Company's concession granted by the Mexican government, as well as amortization of finite life intangible assets. The increase in Depreciation and amortization expense in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to a larger depreciable asset base as a result of capital program spending.

The increase in Depreciation and amortization expense in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to a larger depreciable asset base as a result of capital program spending, partially offset by the favourable impact of the change in FX rates of $9 million.

nonop.heading: Other (Income) Expense
nonop.text:
Other (income) expense consists of gains and losses from the change in FX rates on cash and working capital, financing costs, shareholder costs, equity earnings, and other non-operating expenditures. Other income was $5 million in the third quarter of 2026, a change of $13 million, or 163%, from Other expense of $8 million in the same period of 2025. This change was driven by higher equity income and a net FX gain of $5 million primarily from the re-measurement of working capital denominated in U.S. dollars and Mexican pesos.

Other expense was $1 million in the first nine months of 2026, a change of $2 million, or 200%, from Other income of $1 million in the same period of 2025. This change was driven by net FX losses of $24 million primarily from the re-measurement of working capital and cash denominated in U.S. dollars and Mexican pesos, partially offset by higher equity income.

net sales.heading: Operating Revenues
net sales.text: The Company’s revenues are primarily derived from transporting freight. Changes in freight volumes generally contribute to corresponding changes in Freight revenues and certain variable expenses such as fuel, equipment rents, and crew costs. Non-freight revenues are generated from leasing certain assets, interline switching, and other arrangements including contracts with passenger service operators, subsurface and mineral rights agreements, and logistical services.

Grain.heading: Grain
Grain.text:
The increase in Grain revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to higher volumes of Canadian grain to Vancouver, British Columbia ("B.C."), Mexico, and Thunder Bay, Ontario, higher volumes of U.S. grain to Mexico and the U.S. Pacific Northwest, and an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, the favourable impact of the change in FX rates, and higher freight rates. RTMs increased more than carloads due to moving higher volumes of Grain to Mexico, which has a longer length of haul.

The increase in Grain revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to higher volumes of Canadian grain to Vancouver, Mexico, eastern Canada, and the U.S. Midwest, higher volumes of U.S. grain to Mexico and the U.S. Pacific Northwest, and an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates.

Intermodal.heading: Intermodal
Intermodal.text:
The increase in Intermodal revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM, higher international intermodal volumes to and from the Port of Vancouver and the Port of Montréal, and higher domestic intermodal wholesale volumes, partially offset by lower international intermodal volumes to and from the Port of Saint John. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates.

The increase in Intermodal revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM, higher international intermodal volumes to and from the Port of Vancouver, and higher domestic intermodal wholesale volumes, partially offset by lower international intermodal volumes to and from the Port of Saint John. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates.

Energy, chemicals and plastics.heading: Energy, Chemicals and Plastics
Energy, chemicals and plastics.text:
The increase in Energy, chemicals and plastics revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of liquefied petroleum gas, partially offset by lower volumes of crude. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, the favourable impact of the change in FX rates, and higher freight rates.

The increase in Energy, chemicals and plastics revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of crude, partially offset by lower volumes of fuel oil. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates.

Metals, minerals and consumer products.heading: Metals, Minerals and Consumer Products
Metals, minerals and consumer products.text:
The increase in Metals, minerals and consumer products revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to higher volumes of steel and aluminum and an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, the favourable impact of the change in FX rates, and higher freight rates.

The increase in Metals, minerals and consumer products revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to higher volumes of steel, sand and stone, and aluminum and an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates. RTMs increased more than carloads due to moving higher volumes of sand and stone from Wisconsin to Mexico, which has a longer length of haul.

Automotive.heading: Automotive
Automotive.text:
The increase in Automotive revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM, partially offset by lower volumes from the U.S. Midwest and Mexico. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, the favourable impact of the change in FX rates, and higher freight rates.

The increase in Automotive revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes from Mexico to Canada, partially offset by lower volumes from the U.S. Midwest. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates. Carloads decreased while RTMs increased due to moving lower volumes from Ontario to Chicago and New York, which have shorter lengths of haul, and moving higher volumes from Mexico to Canada, which has a longer length of haul.

Coal.heading: Coal
Coal.text:
Coal revenue was relatively flat in the third quarter of 2026 primarily due to lower volumes of Canadian coal to Kamloops, B.C. and Vancouver, as well as lower volumes of U.S. coal, offset by an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates. RTMs decreased more than carloads due to moving proportionately lower volumes of Canadian coal, which has a longer length of haul.

The decrease in Coal revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to lower volumes of Canadian coal to Kamloops, Vancouver, and Thunder Bay due to lower production and maintenance at both the mines and the ports, as well as lower volumes of U.S. coal, partially offset by an increase in freight revenue per RTM due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates. RTMs decreased more than carloads due to moving proportionately lower volumes of Canadian coal, which has a longer length of haul.

Forest products.heading: Forest Products
Forest products.text:
The increase in Forest products revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of printing papers, wood pulp, and logs and poles, partially offset by lower volumes of paperboard. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, the favourable impact of the change in FX rates, and higher freight rates.

The decrease in Forest products revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to lower volumes of wood pulp, paperboard, and newsprint , partially offset by higher volumes of printing papers and an increase in freight revenue per RTM. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates. Carloads decreased more than RTMs due to moving lower volumes of paperboard from Louisiana to the U.S. Midwest, which has a shorter length of haul.

Potash.heading: Potash
Potash.text:
The increase in Potash revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of export potash to Kansas City, Missouri, Chicago, Illinois, and Kamloops, partially offset by lower volumes of export potash to the U.S. Pacific Northwest and Vancouver and lower volumes of domestic potash. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates.

The increase in Potash revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of export potash to Kansas City and Kamloops, partially offset by lower volumes of export potash to the U.S. Pacific Northwest and Vancouver and lower volumes of domestic potash. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates.

Fertilizers and sulphur.heading: Fertilizers and Sulphur
Fertilizers and sulphur.text:
The increase in Fertilizers and sulphur revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of dry fertilizers, partially offset by lower volumes of sulphur and wet fertilizers. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates. RTMs decreased more than carloads due to moving lower volumes of sulphur from Alberta to Chicago, which has a longer length of haul, and higher volumes of dry fertilizers within Alberta, which has a shorter length of haul.

The increase in Fertilizers and sulphur revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was primarily due to an increase in freight revenue per RTM and higher volumes of dry fertilizers, partially offset by lower volumes of sulphur. Freight revenue per RTM increased due to higher fuel surcharge revenue and higher freight rates, partially offset by the unfavourable impact of the change in FX rates. RTMs decreased while carloads increased due to moving lower volumes of sulphur from Alberta to Chicago, which has a longer length of haul, and higher volumes of dry fertilizers within Alberta, which has a shorter length of haul.

Freight.heading: Freight Revenue per RTM
Freight.text: Freight revenue per RTM is defined as freight revenue per revenue-producing ton of freight over a distance of one mile. This is an indicator of yield. The increase in freight revenue per RTM in the third quarter of 2026 was primarily due to the favourable impact of higher fuel prices on fuel surcharge revenue of $244 million, higher freight rates, and the favourable impact of the change in foreign exchange ("FX") rates of $65 million.

lines.name: Cash and cash equivalents
lines.why: Cash can repay debt or be paid out: a financial asset. Cash needed to run the business is operating; move it if you know how much.

lines.name: Receivables
lines.why: Owed by customers for sales: operating.

lines.name: Prepaid and other current assets
lines.why: Prepayments and other operating items: operating.

lines.name: Property, plant and equipment
lines.why: Assets used to produce and sell: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets
lines.why: Leased stores, offices and equipment used in the business: operating.

lines.name: Goodwill
lines.why: Paid for acquired businesses: operating.

lines.name: Intangible assets
lines.why: Acquired technology, brands and customer relationships: operating.

lines.name: Equity-method investments
lines.why: Stakes in associated businesses, usually part of operations. Financial if held as an investment.

lines.name: Other non-current assets
lines.why: Other long-term operating items: operating.

lines.name: Accounts payable
lines.why: Owed to suppliers for operations: operating.

lines.name: Accrued liabilities
lines.why: Wages, services and other costs not yet paid: operating.

lines.name: Deferred revenue
lines.why: Customers' payments ahead of delivery: operating.

lines.name: Income taxes payable
lines.why: Taxes on operating income: operating.

lines.name: Other current liabilities
lines.why: Other operating items due within a year: operating.

lines.name: Short-term debt and commercial paper
lines.why: Borrowed money: financial.

lines.name: Current portion of long-term debt
lines.why: Borrowed money falling due within a year: financial.

lines.name: Long-term debt
lines.why: Bonds, notes and loans: financial.

lines.name: Operating lease liabilities
lines.why: Rent owed on leases used in the business: operating by default. Move it to financing to treat leases like debt (if the balance sheet has no lease line of its own, they sit inside other liabilities).

lines.name: Deferred tax liabilities
lines.why: Taxes on operating income deferred: operating.

intro.text: Canadian Pacific Kansas City Limited ("CPKC" or the "Company") owns and operates the only freight railway spanning Canada, the United States ("U.S."), and Mexico. CPKC provides rail and intermodal transportation services over a network of approximately 20,000 miles, serving principal business centres across Canada, the U.S., and Mexico. CPKC transports bulk commodities, merchandise freight, and intermodal traffic. For additional information regarding CPKC's network and geographical locations, refer to Item 2. Properties. The Company was originally incorporated on June 22, 2001, under the Canada Business Corporations Act and controls and owns all of the Common Shares of Canadian Pacific Railway Company ("CPRC"), which was incorporated in 1881 by Letters Patent pursuant to an Act of the Parliament of Canada.
